# Part I: Base Model Formation {#part-foundations .unnumbered}

> "The loss scales as a power-law with model size, dataset size, and the amount
> of compute used for training."
>
> Jared Kaplan et al., ["Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models"](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.08361)

The map from Part 0 becomes material here. Before there is an assistant, a tool
call, or a product surface, someone has already chosen how much compute to
spend, what text counts as training data, how that text becomes tokens (the
integer pieces text is cut into, @sec-tokenization), what transformer block
(the repeated layer that turns a sequence into computation) will process those
tokens, and how the run will survive long enough to become a model. These
choices come early, and they set the shape of everything that follows.

Part I is the formation of the base model, where later freedoms are bought and
later constraints are locked in.
@sec-scaling-laws explains why the scale of a training run is decided before
the model exists. @sec-data-curation and @sec-tokenization show how raw web text
is filtered into a training distribution, and why the tokenizer's vocabulary is
part of the model's interface.
The blocks that turn sequence into computation are the work of
@sec-transformer-architecture and @sec-moe-ssm-hybrids: the dense path, the
sparse path, and the long-context alternatives that keep returning under new
names.
@sec-training-at-scale then brings the abstraction back to the cluster:
precision, parallelism, communication, checkpoints, and the many ways a run can
fail without producing anything useful. @sec-mid-training closes the part by
showing what happens after the first broad pass over the web but before
post-training: high-quality annealing, domain bridges, specialist continuation,
and context extension, all of them changes to the data mix and training schedule
rather than to the objective.

Alongside how pre-training works, the part asks which decisions can still be
changed later and which have already become part of the model. Serving,
adaptation, evaluation, and safety all inherit answers from here. Some of those
answers are mathematical, some are engineering compromises, and some are limits
imposed by the hardware.
